opus-5.5.text:
I think of a paper less as a final product and more as a compressed snapshot of a much messier process. When you read a paper, everything looks clean: there's a motivation, a method, a table where the bold numbers are in the right column. But the actual research involved months of wrong turns, failed experiments, and intuitions that changed along the way. Almost none of that makes it onto the page. So in one sense, a paper is a rather lossy medium.

At the same time, I think the format still matters a lot, because it forces you to be honest with yourself. When you sit down to write, you have to ask: what is the one idea here? Can I state it in a sentence? If I can't, maybe I don't understand my own work yet. For me, writing is part of the thinking, not just a report you produce afterward.

What worries me is that, in our field especially, papers have become units of currency. People count them, conferences have tens of thousands of submissions, and there's pressure to slice ideas thinly or optimize for whatever reviewers want to see, usually some benchmark number. When that happens, a paper stops being about communicating knowledge and becomes about signaling. You can read a whole page of results and come away knowing very little about why something works.

The papers I love, the ones that stick with people for years, usually do something different. They share a way of seeing a problem. Maybe the method gets replaced within a year, but the perspective survives. So when I write now, I try to ask what the reader should still remember five years later, even if every number in the tables is obsolete. If there's a good answer to that, the paper is doing its job as a medium. If not, it's probably just a record that we ran some experiments.

I also think papers aren't the only medium anymore. Code releases, blog posts, talks, even conversations like this one carry a lot of the tacit knowledge papers leave out. Ideally they complement each other: the paper is the formal, citable core, and the rest fills in the human story of how the idea actually came about.

r001.rationale: The response considers the reader’s perspective by asking what the reader should still remember five years later.

r002.rationale: It discusses clarifying the paper’s central idea, but does not clearly say the paper should help readers grasp that idea smoothly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I actually think about a lot, because I feel like the paper has been stretched into doing too many jobs at once.

Fundamentally, a paper is supposed to be a vessel for an idea. Someone had an insight, they tested it, and now they want to transfer that insight into another person's head as faithfully and efficiently as possible. That's the ideal. And when it works, it's beautiful. Think about the original ResNet paper, or Transformers, or even older ones like the LeNet or backprop papers. You read them and the core idea is almost embarrassingly simple once you see it. The paper exists to make the simple thing visible.

But in practice, the paper has also become a unit of credit. It's how you get hired, how you get promoted, how a PhD student proves they exist. And once a medium becomes a credential, it starts to distort. You see papers padded with tables, with eight ablations that don't change the story, with language designed to sound more novel than the work actually is. The communication function and the credentialing function are pulling in opposite directions.

I try to tell my students that the best papers are the ones where you can summarize the contribution in one sentence, and the rest of the paper is just honest evidence for that sentence. If you can't do that, either the idea isn't ready or you haven't understood it yet. A lot of what I do in the writing process is actually subtraction. What can I remove so the reader sees the thing I saw?

The other thing I'd say is that the paper is no longer the only medium, and maybe not even the primary one. Code, model weights, a good blog post, a Twitter thread, a talk with the right figure in it. Sometimes a single well-designed figure does more communicating than ten pages of text. I think a lot about the figure first, before the writing. If the figure doesn't tell the story, the paper won't either.

So I'd put it this way. The paper is still the archival record, the thing that has to be rigorous and reproducible. But it's a somewhat slow and heavy medium, and we shouldn't pretend it's the only way knowledge actually moves in this field anymore. The ideas that really spread are the ones that are simple enough to survive outside the paper.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes transferring an insight into a reader’s head and removing material so the reader can see the central idea, expressing a reader-focused view of papers.

r002.rationale: It describes a paper’s purpose as helping another person grasp the author’s insight faithfully and efficiently, with the rest serving as evidence for that idea.

astra-6.text:
I think a paper is a very useful medium, but it’s a compressed version of the research process. You spend months exploring a problem, trying things that don’t work, changing your assumptions. Then you turn that into a few pages with a clear motivation, a method, and results. That structure makes the work easier to communicate, but it also hides a lot of how you actually arrived there.

For me, the most valuable thing a paper can communicate is the thinking behind the work. Why is this the right question to ask? What observation led to this particular design? What did we learn that might still matter even if the method itself gets replaced? Ideally, the reader walks away with something they can use to think about their own problems.

And that’s where conversation can complement a paper. You can ask why someone abandoned an idea, where they were confused, or which result surprised them. Those details don’t always fit into the final narrative, but they can be very useful for understanding the research.

r001.rationale: It discusses what a paper communicates and what readers can take away, but does not convey that papers should be considered from the readers’ perspective.

r002.rationale: It says a paper’s clear structure makes research easier to communicate, but does not frame the paper as helping readers smoothly grasp the author’s central idea.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a paper is a very useful medium, but it’s also a compressed representation of the research process. You spend months exploring something, trying ideas that don’t work, changing your assumptions. Then you turn that into a few pages with a clean narrative: here’s the problem, here’s the method, here are the results. That makes it easier to communicate, but it can hide how the understanding actually developed.

For me, the most valuable thing a paper can communicate is an insight. What did you learn, and why should someone else care? The method and the experiments should help the reader understand that insight and judge whether the evidence supports it.

And ideally, the paper gives you something you can carry into your own work. You might never use the exact model or reproduce the exact experiment, but it changes how you think about a problem. That’s a powerful form of communication.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes making the paper easier for readers to understand and letting them judge the evidence, expressing a reader-focused view of the paper.

r002.rationale: It says the paper should communicate an insight and that its method and experiments should help readers understand that insight.
